t: Graph Connectivity With Threshold: Sieve-Style Union-Find
o: City labels x and y share a road exactly when gcd(x, y) exceeds threshold, yet a query succeeds through ANY chain of roads, not just direct ones — so per-query gcd checks are both wrong and too slow. In Example 1 (n = 6, threshold = 2), cities 3 and 6 share divisor 3 so [3, 6] is true, while 1 has no divisor above 2 and none of 2, 4, 5 finds an eligible partner, so [1, 4] and [2, 5] are false. What we need is the component structure of this implicit divisor graph, computed once before answering up to 10^5 queries. The key reframing mirrors the Sieve of Eratosthenes: every integer z > threshold makes ALL of its multiples mutually connected, because any two multiples share z. Unioning z with each of its multiples costs roughly n/z steps, and summed over all z that harmonic total is O(n log n) — comfortably within limits.
k: Many connectivity queries over a static graph point to Union-Find: build components once, answer each query by comparing roots.
Think sieve, not pairs: for each z > threshold union z with all its multiples; the work totals the harmonic sum O(n log n).
gcd(a, b) > threshold per query fails because cities may connect indirectly through intermediate cities.

a.n: Approach 1: Build the Explicit Graph, Then Search Per Query
a.i: The literal translation of the statement: draw an undirected edge between every pair whose gcd exceeds threshold, then BFS for every query. It is obviously correct and easy to reason about, but n = 10^4 means roughly 5 * 10^7 pairs each needing a gcd call, plus a potentially huge BFS per query. Treat it as the correctness baseline the optimized version must match.
s: For every pair 1 <= x < y <= n, add edge x-y when gcd(x, y) > threshold.
For each query, BFS from ai marking reachable cities.
Answer true iff bi was marked.
a.t: O(n^2 log n + Q * (n + m)) — pairwise gcd computations dominate the build, then each query runs its own search.
a.sp: O(n^2) — adjacency storage for potentially quadratic edges.

a.i: Replace pairwise checks with divisor-centric merging, exactly like replacing trial division with a sieve. For fixed z > threshold the cities z, 2z, 3z, ... form one connected group, so a single pass of unions per z captures every road whose common divisor is z. Starting at threshold + 1 and stopping the outer loop at floor(n / 2) — larger z has no proper multiple inside n — keeps the operation count at the harmonic sum, about n ln n, while path-halving finds stay effectively constant.
s: Initialize a disjoint-set forest over labels 1..n.
For each z from threshold + 1 to floor(n / 2), union z with every multiple w = 2z, 3z, ... up to n.
For each query [a, b], return find(a) == find(b).
a.t: O(n log n + Q * α(n)) — harmonic-sum sieve unions dominate preprocessing; each query costs two finds.
a.sp: O(n) — one parent entry per city.

w: Sketch the pairwise-BFS idea to show understanding, then deliver the sieve + Union-Find solution — that combination reads best in an interview. Classic pitfall: answering with gcd(a, b) > threshold ignores multi-hop connectivity. Subtle points worth mentioning: the outer loop stops at floor(n/2) because bigger z has no proper multiple, and z itself never unions with anything. Likely follow-ups: per-query thresholds (answer offline in descending threshold order, activating unions incrementally), or dynamic deletions, where plain Union-Find breaks down and link-cut trees or offline divide-and-conquer take over.
